item.content:encoded:
Artificial intelligence has changed cybersecurity permanently. While OpenAI’s inadvertent attack on Hugging Face brought AI-generated attacks to everyone’s attention, AI has been on security professionals’ radar for a long time. AI makes attacks possible at a scale that was hard to imagine a few years ago. Newly discovered zero-days can be exploited almost immediately. Deepfakes and their implications for phishing, vishing, and other attacks were nightmares that we knew were real; we just hoped we’d have a few more years before we needed to defend against them. And of course, inattention to security at OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and other labs that we don’t yet know about has resulted in AI agents that attack other systems in an attempt to solve a problem.

While the headlines have been shouting about AI killing humanity, doomsday AI is more likely a smokescreen to divert attention away from real harms that are happening now. We don’t need panic. We need an assessment of where we are: What are the threats? Where are the skills gaps? Where is the budget? It’s hard to overstate the importance of these questions; Tomasz Tunguz, writing about the Theory 2026 AI Survey, reports that security is the biggest barrier to AI adoption. To start answering these questions, in September we ran a survey that asked infosec professionals about the intersection between artificial intelligence and security. 351 respondents completed the full survey, 209 of whom self-identified as being involved with security as part of their job. This report focuses on those 209 respondents.

Attacks, risks, and responses

52% of respondents said their work rarely (34%) or never (18%) involves AI-generated attacks. This seems unlikely. The most likely explanation is that the security profession includes a broad range of job responsibilities; many security professionals don’t deal directly with defense. That group includes auditors, security experts on software development teams, strategists, architects, and others. It’s also possible that most phishes are either blocked by an automated filter (itself an instance of AI) or deleted immediately by the recipient; many companies require their staff to take training courses that cover topics like recognizing phishes. Still, it’s surprising. Much simpler versions of AI have been used to generate spam and phishing email for years. AI’s ability to generate phishes was demonstrated at BlackHat in 2021 with GPT-3. It’s been part of the security picture for a long time.

The most commonly observed attacks are AI-generated phishing (55%), vulnerability scanning and exploitation (30%), and AI-assisted malware generation (26%). Respondents who frequently encountered AI attacks also reported more types of attacks. There’s no surprise here: If you see attacks more frequently, you are more likely to observe specific attacks. The strongest relationship was with AI-generated phishing, which was seen by 55% of all respondents and 86% of those who observed AI-generated attacks weekly. Among respondents who observed attacks daily, slightly fewer (78%) reported phishing. Given the small sample, the difference may not be meaningful. It’s also likely that respondents who observe attacks daily are seeing a much broader range of attacks and that phishing is genuinely less important to them.

Respondents reported seeing deepfake audio and video, which can be used for vishing and other impersonation attacks, less often than phishing, though it was far from nonexistent (25%). More respondents than we expected reported fully automated attacks, like OpenAI’s attack on Hugging Face, though the percentage was still low (16%). The percentage of respondents who observed adversarial inputs against models including prompt injection was similarly low (only 13%), but that’s high enough to indicate that prompt injection and other attacks directed against models are a real concern.

When we asked respondents what AI-related risks concerned them most, we got a different set of answers. The two most common concerns were overreliance on AI tools without human verification and leaking sensitive data via AI tools; 49% of respondents selected each answer. (The number of respondents selecting those answers happened to be the same, though there was little relationship between the two groups.) 

Although the quality of AI output has gotten a lot better in the past year, relying on unverified AI outputs remains problematic. However, AI can easily generate more output than humans are capable of reviewing, and software teams are now overwhelmed by the volume of AI-generated pull requests that need human review before they can be merged. This overload is causing many to rethink the review process and others to reject AI-generated PRs. Code review was never very good at finding bugs; it was better at familiarizing a team with developments in the codebase. It may be enough to rely on exhaustive testing.

Understanding how your software works when much of it is written by AI is a deeper problem. While AI is good at answering questions about a codebase, it usually doesn’t have access to the reasoning behind the code, which is often hidden in institutional knowledge—and institutional knowledge often means “Oh, yeah, that guy who retired three years ago.” In addition, software developers may lose their programming skills if writing code becomes a smaller part of their job. Security professionals themselves might wonder whether relying on AI for red-teaming, log analysis, and vulnerability detection leads to a degradation in their own skills. 

Companies also fear losing sensitive data via AI. Most AI providers offer enterprise accounts that promise that they won’t train models on data in prompts or attached documents, but it’s not clear that these terms of service can be trusted. The frontier laboratories are getting increasingly desperate for training data, even going to lengths such as buying failing startups for their data. Read OpenAI’s description of its Zero Data Retention and Private Safety Processing cynically, and ask if this really protects corporate data or if it allows using data in ways that aren’t directly observable by humans—for example, automatically generating synthetic data. Security professionals are paid to be cynical; thinking about how software, protocols, and policies can be abused is part of the job.

Roughly a third (35%) of the respondents are concerned about attackers using AI to discover vulnerabilities faster than they can mitigate those vulnerabilities and apply patches. Updating software is usually a good practice, but it comes with its own risks: Software updates may introduce new bugs and can lead to incompatibilities with established tools and practices. And defenders can’t yet delegate vulnerability detection, patching, and updating to AI. So overall, is AI more of a help to defenders or attackers? Andrew Ng, Bruce Schneier, and others have argued that the attackers are ahead right now. It’s easier to find a vulnerability, use it to create a payload, and launch an attack than it is to stop one. But the balance will eventually shift to the defenders, as AI becomes more capable of finding and patching vulnerabilities before they can become a problem.

It’s surprising that only a quarter (25%) of the respondents listed AI-generated phishing as a top concern, especially since phishing is the attack most frequently seen in the wild. Perhaps we’ve become too used to phishing; we’ve all been to the security trainings, we’ve all experienced it directly, and some of us have even fallen victim. Phishing is also an attack that, in many cases, is handled automatically. Familiarity may not always breed contempt, but something you see almost daily usually isn’t your biggest worry. 

More exotic attacks are even less of a concern. Only 11% listed prompt injection as one of their top concerns, for instance. However, real-world examples of prompt injection are appearing with increasing frequency. A recent study observed that roughly 1% of résumés contained hidden text to trick an AI system. Google has noticed many kinds of prompt injection, ranging from benign to overtly hostile. And in 2025, OWASP recognized prompt injection as the greatest security risk for users of AI. It’s surprising and unfortunate that it doesn’t appear to be a greater concern for security professionals, especially since prompt injection is a vulnerability that might be lessened by careful filtering but can’t be eliminated.

Even fewer security professionals are concerned about data poisoning (4%). Data poisoning is a serious problem for organizations that train their own models, but today frontier labs conduct much of the most resource-intensive model training. However, this is changing as post-training on corporate data becomes more common. We believe the trend toward locally specialized models will continue, and that data poisoning, as distinct from data theft, will become more of a concern. 

We asked specifically about the use of agents, which exploded this year with the launch of OpenClaw and Gas Town in January 2026. Agents create another set of security concerns. We’ve all heard horror stories: agents that deleted production databases, handled data improperly, generated email that should never have been sent, and the like. Using an agent properly requires a lot of attention to detail, and many users aren’t used to that responsibility, nor do they understand security well enough to exercise responsibility.

The biggest concern among our respondents is excessive permissions or unclear ownership (28%). That’s hardly a surprise; many security problems trace back to permissions. Unclear ownership makes permissions issues more dangerous. When an agent is making many calls to a model, using tools, and delegating to other agents and models, it quickly becomes unclear who (or what) is the authority responsible for any action. This situation isn’t handled well by our current authentication and authorization systems, which assume that identities and authorizations are long-term, stable entities.

Lack of monitoring or auditability was the second highest concern (19%), followed by inability to verify whether the agent stayed within its role (18%). These concerns are closely related: Ownership is often unclear when agents are in use, and lack of monitoring makes the situation worse. Likewise, when you can’t monitor, it’s difficult, if not impossible, to verify whether the agents stayed in their lane—and we’ve seen all too many examples recently of agents that abandoned their authorized roles in inappropriate ways.

Data leakage appears again, though it’s surprisingly low on the list (15%) given that 49% of the respondents indicated that data leakage was one of their top concerns. It’s possible that we’re seeing the difference between single and multiple selection questions; many respondents are concerned about data leakage, but it’s not their top concern. 

Prompt injection doesn’t rank highly for either question: 9% selected it as their top concern about AI agents, and 11% selected it as one of their top concerns. 

Policies and funding

Although nearly three-quarters of the respondents reported that their companies have an AI use policy in place (72%), less than half (44%) reported that the security policy is “comprehensive,” while 28% said that the policy is basic and needs updating. Another 9% said that their employer doesn’t have a policy but is actively developing one. 19% said that there was no policy, or that they “didn’t know,” an answer we consider equivalent to “there is no policy.”

Organizations need clear AI policies that tell employees what AI tools they can use and how they should (and shouldn’t) use them. It’s important for employees to understand whether their company is sensitive to sending data offsite, whether the company’s chosen AI providers guarantee their data won’t be used for training, which practices for attribution are acceptable, and much more. We have some sympathy with organizations that have a basic policy that needs updating. AI’s capabilities are advancing at unprecedented speed; a policy that was adequate in 2023 certainly needs updating now, and a policy that’s only a year old still predates the widespread use of agents like OpenClaw, Claude Code, and Codex, along with the widespread use of skills and tools to extend an agent’s capabilities. Keeping a policy up-to-date with the current state of AI is an imposing task.

The existence of a policy appears to be related to whether employees use AI safely. We asked about “shadow AI” (the use of AI outside of any definitive policy) and found that 36% of the respondents thought that their teammates occasionally use “shadow AI” and 23% thought that the practice is widespread. About a quarter (24%) thought that shadow AI use is rare; and 16% were unsure. 

The relationship between shadow AI and the existence of an AI policy tells us a lot about whether policies are effective. Respondents with a comprehensive AI policy were more likely to say that shadow AI use is rare (37%) or that it’s only used occasionally (36%); only 17% said that shadow AI is widespread at their company. In contrast, 35% of the respondents who reported a basic policy said that shadow AI is widespread—almost the same percentage as those who reported that there was no policy at all (37%) and only slightly worse than those who said that a policy is in development but doesn’t exist yet (28%). Those who had a basic policy, a policy under development, or no policy were less likely to report that shadow AI was used “rarely or never” (13%, 6%, and 21%, respectively).

Granted that shadow AI is probably underreported across the board, our data clearly shows that a comprehensive AI policy is a powerful tool in limiting it. If the policy is poor, or it doesn’t exist, employees will use whatever tools they can to get their job done, which leads to AI use that’s inconsistent, insecure, and possibly counterproductive; it may even lead to legal, contractual, and reputational risks. When there’s no policy, it’s also likely that AI isn’t used as widely as it could be. Telling employees what is expected helps them to act responsibly. A good AI policy doesn’t just tell staff what not to do; it also communicates how to use AI in ways that are appropriate, and may even provide for training. 

When we asked whether organizations are adequately funding AI security, the picture was better than we expected. The largest group (32%) said that AI security is sufficiently funded, and 28% said it’s partially funded. Only 16% said it is severely underfunded, and 23% are unsure. I admit to being surprised by this result. Security is often underfunded, partly because a successful year is one in which “nothing bad happened,” and “we need to spend more so that nothing bad will continue to happen” isn’t a story that plays well at budget time. But executives have been catching on over the last few decades; high-profile attacks and data thefts lead to CIOs and CISOs losing their jobs, and that’s enough to get anyone’s attention. 

We saw a strong link between a comprehensive AI policy and adequate funding for security. Nearly half (49%) of the respondents who said their company has a comprehensive AI policy also said that AI security is sufficiently funded, and another 29% said that it’s partially funded. Only 3% of this group said that AI security is severely underfunded. That means nearly 80% (78%) are at least partially satisfied with funding.

Once again, the answers given by respondents who said that their organizations have a basic policy, a policy under development, or no policy were surprisingly similar. 16%, 22%, and 21%, respectively, said that AI security is sufficiently funded. That’s certainly not a vote of confidence, though we might be able to draw two more bits of information from it. Developing a policy looks like it’s slightly better than having an out-of-date policy; the company is putting in the effort and making an investment. That makes some intuitive sense, though it might also be wishful thinking. Among respondents whose organizations have a basic policy, the largest subgroup said that AI security is partially funded (42%). A middle-of-the-road policy is associated with middle-of-the-road funding. Is that fair, or is that what reality looks like?

Tools and skills

While AI gives security professionals powerful new tools, they aren’t yet fully taking advantage of them. Two-thirds of the respondents (68%) reported that they use a chat, copilot, or similar tool for research or documentation. But only slightly over a third use AI to scan for vulnerabilities (38%), just over a quarter use it for threat detection (27%), and a quarter use AI for incident response (25%). Security professionals widely use general-purpose AI. However, those using specialized tools like vulnerability scanners remain the minority.

To probe further, we asked where AI improved respondents’ workflows. More than half said that AI improved their workflows for research or documentation (61%) and that it reduced repetitive work (57%). But only 29% said that AI improved their workflow for triage, and 17% said that it improved detection accuracy. These results confirm what we saw for tool use.

The relationship between tool use and impact shows up even more clearly when we look at who’s benefiting most from AI. Those who are only using chat or a copilot see the greatest improvement in the speed of research or documentation. Chatbots and copilots save time, particularly when writing reports with a lot of boilerplate text, but they aren’t as helpful when actively defending against or recovering from attacks. Without specialized tools, that work has to be manual.

Respondents using security-specific AI tools were more likely to report improvements in alert triage (42% versus 18%) and detection accuracy (27% versus 5%) than those using only general-purpose chatbots or copilots. 

It’s far from surprising that respondents who didn’t use any AI tools were most likely to say that they saw no noticeable positive impact. The bigger question is why they saw any impact at all. 

Finally, we looked at the “skills gap” to determine what skills and tools would make respondents more effective. Only 7% of the respondents said that they don’t feel like they have a skills gap; that group was also the most likely to say that they aren’t using any AI tools. It’s clear that most of our respondents see AI as a necessary part of the future and want to be part of it. 

34% of the respondents want to use AI tools more effectively. That desire was evenly spread across all AI users, both chat/copilot only (36%) and users of security-specific tools (37%). 24% want to learn how to use AI to secure systems (including the use of AI for red-teaming); 19% want to learn AI-specific attack techniques; and 12% want to learn how to detect AI-generated attacks. 

The future of security

We started by claiming that AI has changed computer security forever. In addition to the many reports of research projects that inadvertently attacked other sites, AI has become a tool for attackers. They aren’t distracted by arguments about whether or not AI is taking jobs; their goal is to exploit their victims, and it’s clear that AI will help them. And as Ben Lorica points out in his newsletter, the economics of attack are changing: AI is infinitely patient, can try multiple attack vectors, can abandon failures, and can work at a scale that’s difficult for humans to match.

AI is also a tool for defenders. We saw more security professionals using AI than we expected, though not as many as we had hoped. Many defenders are taking advantage of chatbots and copilots but haven’t yet adopted more specialized tools, which are associated with improvements in workflows for triage and threat detection. 

The tools for defenders undoubtedly need to mature, but tools aren’t the entire answer. Organizations that adopt AI successfully will have appropriate budgets and policies for AI use; they will understand the risks that come with AI adoption; they will proactively fill skills gaps; and they will recognize processes that are no longer productive and “turn scar tissue into infrastructure.” AI is, in the end, a “normal technology” that takes years to penetrate organizations, as Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor have argued. Tools, budgets, and thought processes all need to change, and that takes time. Getting ahead of the curve on AI won’t happen if individuals work in isolation, adopting tools and ideas as they see fit. It’s an effort that requires the entire organization.

item.title: The Second-User Test
item.dc:creator: Kaiyao Duan
item.custom:subtitle: AI can make the first version work. What happens when someone else tries to use it?
item.description: In my work with G7–G12 students at Force Academy, a research initiative in Chongqing, I sometimes take a project that appears to be finished and give another student responsibility for using, checking, or modifying it. The handoff is a test of understanding: Can the work still make sense when its creator is no longer there […]
item.content:encoded:
In my work with G7–G12 students at Force Academy, a research initiative in Chongqing, I sometimes take a project that appears to be finished and give another student responsibility for using, checking, or modifying it. The handoff is a test of understanding: Can the work still make sense when its creator is no longer there to translate it? The original author knows what every variable means, why a particular decision was made, which tool was used, and which parts can safely be changed. The second student has only what the project makes visible.

Generative AI makes the handoff more revealing because it lowers the cost of producing a convincing first version. Students can generate code, analysis, prose, visualizations, and prototypes far more quickly than they could a few years ago. In a classroom, however, a project is useful only insofar as it shows what the student understands and can defend. AI can supply missing code, smooth over incomplete reasoning, or turn a rough idea into fluent prose, so polish is no longer strong evidence of understanding by itself.

A concrete example came from a student paper on AI and labor economics, Verification Responsibility in AI-Applicable Occupations. The paper asked what remains economically important when AI makes candidate outputs cheap but a person still has to check those outputs, decide whether they are safe to use, and remain responsible for accepting them.

The lead student developed the conceptual model and most of the analytical workflow. A second student was given a narrower job: rerun the main analyses independently, record the versions of the source data, document how occupations in one dataset were linked to occupations in another, and compare the reported tables and figures with the underlying outputs. What looked like procedural verification quickly became a substantive review of the study.

The first problem was reproducibility. The analysis ran on the original machine, but too much of the workflow depended on choices that lived in one student’s memory. To reproduce it elsewhere, the team had to record the data transformations, write down the rules for linking occupational datasets, and keep intermediate results so another person could see how the final numbers had been produced rather than simply rerunning a script and trusting the output.

The more consequential problem was in the measurement design. An early version of the study used some of the same autonomy and leadership survey items in two different measures: verification responsibility and adaptive capacity. The software had calculated the relationship between those measures correctly, but part of the apparent relationship could have been created by the fact that the two measures shared some of the same inputs. In other words, the code was doing what it had been asked to do; the question was whether the quantities being compared had been defined cleanly enough.

The team rebuilt the measures so they no longer shared survey items, removed ambiguous items, and revised the workflow so source versions, cross-dataset links, exclusions, intermediate files, and reported results could be traced. Later versions added alternative specifications and robustness checks. What began as “please rerun this” ended up forcing a redesign of the study.

The handoff changed how I read student work. A second user does not merely test whether the files have been packaged neatly; they ask the awkward questions the creator may have stopped noticing. Why is a particular variable there? Which conclusion depends on an assumption that was never made explicit? In this project, those questions reached back into the measurement design.

The educational value of the handoff comes from the fact that schoolwork and production software have different ends. Professional developers learn a great deal after software leaves their hands because they have to deliver it, explain it, support it, maintain it, and respond when someone uses it in an unexpected way. Student projects usually disappear when a course ends, and that is fine; the artifact is not the goal. What matters is importing some of the learning that comes from delivery and maintenance: explaining decisions, supporting someone else’s use, and revising the work when private context is no longer available.

At Force Academy, the exact task depends on the project. For a computational model, another student may change a parameter or replace one rule and then ask what should remain stable. For an AI-supported workflow, the job may be to move it to a different model or environment. For a data analysis, the second student may try to reconstruct one result from the recorded source files and transformations. When that transfer fails, I want the original student to decide what the other person actually needed to know and what should be changed in the project, rather than simply standing beside them and explaining it.

I use the word “handles” for the visible points of entry that make that possible. A handle gives another person something concrete to inspect or change without first receiving a private briefing. It might be a clearly named parameter, an explicit assumption, a test that records an earlier failure, a replaceable component, a retained intermediate dataset, or a prompt whose important context is written down instead of buried in a private chat history.

Handles also make disagreement more productive. An exposed assumption can be challenged; a component with a clear boundary can be modified or replaced without rebuilding the whole project; and a numerical result linked to its source data and transformations can be checked rather than accepted on authority.

Outside school, AI systems expose the same weakness. A prompt, workflow, skill, or agent configuration may look portable because it can be copied, while the conditions that make it work remain elsewhere: tool access, file structure, model behavior, private memory, naming conventions, or small decisions the creator never needed to document. Moving the artifact often reveals how much of the working system was never inside the artifact in the first place.

A first successful run is therefore weak evidence. It tells me that a particular combination of person, model, tools, data, and context produced an output once. A stronger test is whether another person can reconstruct what matters, distinguish assumptions from implementation details, and make a change without destroying the logic of the work.

Tim O’Reilly’s idea of an architecture of participation gives me the broader frame. A technical artifact becomes more useful when other people can enter it without negotiating privately with its creator. In software, that usually means interfaces, conventions, documentation, modularity, and replaceable components. In data analysis, the same principle shows up as recorded source versions, visible transformations, retained intermediate results, explicit assumptions, and enough analytical logic for someone else to rerun or challenge the work.

For education, the milestone I care about is whether the student understands the work well enough to make some of that understanding available to someone else. A second student who can use, question, and extend the project gives me evidence that a polished first run cannot.

AI expands what one person can build, including what a teenager can attempt without a large technical team. The expanded scope is a real gain, but it also makes successful generation easier to confuse with understanding. When I want to know what a student really understands, I now learn more from the first serious handoff than from the first successful run.

item.title: Building an AI Analyst, One Football Argument at a Time
item.dc:creator: Chester Ismay and Michelle Smith
item.custom:subtitle: Does it pay to establish the run? Here’s what our agent says.
item.description: One of my biggest pet peeves is the Monday morning quarterback, the person who second-guesses every coaching decision after the fact. item.content:encoded:
One of my biggest pet peeves is the Monday morning quarterback, the person who second-guesses every coaching decision after the fact. In The Monday Morning Agent, we’re building one that actually checks the data.

Every other Monday, I’ll take an argument NFL fans can’t stop having and hand it to an AI agent. We’ll use about a quarter-million plays from five complete seasons of public nflverse data, plus the current season as it unfolds. Each of our eight episodes will give the agent another capability. By the finale, it’ll run the desk unattended, and we’ll check what it investigated and what it correctly refused to answer.

We’ll start with “You have to establish the run.” I want the agent to explain what that claim means and what evidence would support it.

Define the claim before querying the data

“Establish the run” can mean that running early pays off late, wearing down the defense, or setting up play action. These are very different claims and they need different data. For this first episode, I focused on whether teams that run more often early in a game win more often.

Before the agent called the tool, I asked it to write one sentence explaining what would have to be true in the data for the claim to hold, including when in the game it applies. “Establish” here means early. A whole-game number doesn’t really test that. Give your agent the same assignment, and check that it’s answering the question you intended.

Give the agent a job you can check

Before any agent touched this, I ran the analysis code myself. The tool did the counting; the agent interpreted the results. Then I wrote the policy in a Markdown file, spelling out its job, the read-only tool it may use, and what its answer needed to include. It has to explain what the plays can’t tell us. It may not say running causes winning.

Try questions outside that job too. When I asked which team I should bet on, the agent refused without calling the tool, because that request is beyond the scope of our agent. But when a viewer asked about running trends, the results got tangled up with the “establish the run” instructions. I had to clarify what I was asking, and still wanted to see the code and validate the answer. As you give an agent more responsibility, check both its results and whether it understood the task.

Make the filters part of the answer

“You have to establish the run” sounds airtight at first. Over the last five seasons, teams with the highest run share, the percentage of their plays that were runs, won 77.7% of their games. Those with the lowest run share won 19.2%. I initially looked at that and thought, “Problem solved, we’re done.” Most of that gap, though, reflects teams that were already ahead running out the clock.

When the agent looked only at first-half running in games within three points at halftime, the result flipped. Teams with the highest first-half run share won 46.3% of the time; those with the lowest won 55.3%. This season through Week 5 points the same way, but each group contained only 11 team games. One game could swing it. That doesn’t mean passing causes winning. We’re measuring association, and the filters change which games we’re comparing.

One filter changed the whole story, which is why the filters have to be on-screen. I wanted to see how many rows remained and which commands produced the results so I could go back and check. Make those details part of your agent’s answer, including when it’s working with a smaller sample.

A few numbers from last week’s games

In Week 5, the team that ran more in the first half won 6 of the 15 games, lost 8, and tied 1 (Giants at Washington). Over the past five seasons that team won 54.3% of the time, so last week came in below the average. That’s not unusual, though. In 27 of the 95 regular-season weeks since 2021, the team that ran more early finished the week with a losing record. One week of games doesn’t say much on its own, which is why the agent reports five seasons alongside the current one.

One more data point: The Monday night game, Buffalo at the Rams, was the first the agent hadn’t seen. Buffalo ran on 60% of its first-half plays to the Rams’ 35%, led by six at halftime, and won by three in overtime. Those 199 plays are in the data now, and the close-at-halftime numbers from the episode didn’t change.

Next up: “Ban the Tush Push”

On October 26, we’ll tackle “Ban the Tush Push.” Not one of the 260,927 play descriptions from 2021 through this season’s October 11 games contains the words “tush push.” After adding Monday night’s game, we have 261,126 descriptions, and “sneak” appears in only two, both from 2021. The data isn’t going to hand us a definition.

Before the agent can judge the play, it has to define it. I’ll challenge it to write that definition into its first permanent document, a shared data dictionary, and cite it in every ruling from then on. Bring your own definition, because the answer depends on which one you pick.

O’Reilly members can sign up on the O’Reilly learning platform to join me live on October 26, 8:00am–8:45am PT / 11:00am–11:45am ET. Everyone can follow along on Radar every other Monday, with a brief pause for the holidays. Watch episode one above, and we’ll build on it in the next session.
